name: Raw vegan diet
lead: A raw vegan diet consists of uncooked plant foods, typically fruit, vegetables, nuts, seeds, sprouts and juices, usually kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius, and excludes all animal products. It is one branch of raw foodism, which also includes versions that eat raw meat, eggs and dairy.[8][10]

People adopt it to look and feel better: clearer-looking skin, a lean body, steady energy and general vitality are the outcomes followers most often describe. The route is practical. Fruit, leafy greens, sprouts and juices are low in energy density and high in fibre, and the diet removes processed and fried foods, so intake of calories and refined ingredients tends to fall.[8][16] Proponents add that cooking destroys enzymes and nutrients, and that eating plants raw keeps their full 'life force'; dietetic sources describe that enzyme claim differently, and the idea has roots in early twentieth-century European nature-cure movements.[10][13]

Research is small and mostly observational. Studies of long-term followers report low vitamin B12 status without supplements, lower body fat and lower cardiometabolic risk markers, better gum health in one comparison, and case reports describing both elite endurance performance and complications in children.[1][2][4][5][7][16] Wellness retreats built on raw vegan eating, such as the Hippocrates Health Institute in Florida, have been the subject of pilot studies of quality of life.[3][6][12] No trial has tested the diet for skin or facial appearance.

The British Dietetic Association has called raw veganism a fad diet, and dietetic sources point to B12, vitamin D and calorie intake as nutrients of concern.[8][10] Related and stricter patterns include fruitarianism, and the diet's online presence includes influencers, bodybuilding forums and communities that compare it with raw animal-food and fruit-and-meat diets.[9][14][17]

paras: Raw vegans eat plant foods that have not been heated above a threshold usually given as 40 to 48 degrees Celsius, though some followers use 42 or 46. Foods are prepared by blending, juicing, sprouting, soaking, fermenting and dehydrating at low temperature. Common dishes include green smoothies, salads, nut-based 'cheeses', raw crackers, sprouted grains and seeds, fruit bowls and cold-pressed juices.[8][10]

Some followers eat 100 percent raw; others aim for a proportion, for instance 75 percent raw, as in the plan popularised by Leslie Kenton's 1984 book Raw Energy.[10] Raw veganism has subgroups: fruitarians eat mostly fruit, juicearians rely on juices, and sproutarians emphasise sprouted seeds and grains.[10] Fruitarian diets are a stricter pattern and are described in dietetic sources as more restrictive than veganism or raw veganism.[14]

In appearance communities the diet is discussed mainly for skin and leanness. Followers say that dropping processed food, sugar-laden snacks and dairy, and eating large amounts of fruit, vegetables and water-rich foods, gives them a clearer complexion, a glow and a slimmer midsection. Observational data fit part of this picture: a cross-sectional study of strict raw food eaters in Germany found lower BMI and body-fat percentage than vegan and omnivore comparison groups.[16] The same study also found lower energy and protein intake, so the leanness comes with a lower intake of several nutrients.[16]

Skin outcomes have not been tested in trials. Followers' reports of skin change are anecdotal, and they are often mixed with the effects of other changes such as weight loss, more water intake and removal of alcohol.[9][18]

Raw eating has religious and ascetic precedents, such as hermits and monks who avoided cooked food.[10] The modern movement is usually traced to Swiss physician Maximilian Bircher-Benner (1867-1939), who after recovering from an illness by eating raw apples began to prescribe raw fruit and vegetables and devised the muesli dish. He founded a Zurich sanatorium called Vital Force, and held that raw plants carry more nutritional value than cooked food or meat, advising healthy people to eat about half their food raw. Critics at the time and later disputed his vitalist reasoning; novelist Thomas Mann called the sanatorium a 'health jail'.[13] Wikipedia dates the sanatorium opening to 1904 in one article and Bircher-Benner's own biography page to 1897.[10][13]

Early English-language advocates included Eugene Christian, whose 1904 book Uncooked Foods and How to Use Them is cited as an early raw-food text, and the Eutropheon, opened in 1917 and described as America's first raw food restaurant.[10] Herbert Shelton, a promoter of natural hygiene, was arrested and fined several times for practising medicine without a licence, and Norman Walker popularised raw juicing in the 1970s.[10]

Ann Wigmore (1909-1994), a Lithuanian-American naturopath, was a central figure in the late twentieth-century 'living foods' movement. From the 1940s she promoted wheatgrass juice and uncooked food for detoxification, citing the healing properties of chlorophyll. Her Boston foundation gained non-profit status in 1970 and was renamed the Hippocrates Health Institute in 1982.[11][12] She was sued by the Massachusetts attorney general in 1982 over claims that her programme could cure diabetes, and again in 1988 over a pamphlet about an 'energy enzyme soup'; a judge ruled her statements were protected speech but barred her from presenting herself as a physician.[11] The institute, co-founded with Viktoras Kulvinskas, moved to West Palm Beach, Florida in 1987 under Brian Clement.[11][12]

Leslie Kenton's Raw Energy (1984) brought a mostly-raw diet to a mainstream readership.[10] In the 21st century, raw eating has had parallel strands online: raw vegan, fruitarian, and raw animal-food versions linked in news coverage to a bodybuilding subculture and the 'primal diet' of Aajonus Vonderplanitz.[10]

Proponents of raw veganism commonly hold several ideas. First, heat above about 40 to 48 degrees inactivates enzymes in food and thereby reduces its value; this 'enzyme' idea is a defining claim of the living-foods tradition.[10][11] Second, raw plants retain more vitamins and phytochemicals than cooked ones. Third, cooking creates compounds such as acrylamide, advanced glycation end products and polycyclic aromatic hydrocarbons that followers wish to avoid.[10] Fourth, many followers describe the diet as 'detoxifying', a notion associated with wheatgrass and juice fasts at Wigmore's institute.[11]

Dietetic and scientific sources respond that food enzymes are themselves digested in the stomach and gut rather than contributing meaningfully to digestion, and that cooking can raise the availability of nutrients such as beta-carotene and vitamin E while reducing others.[10] The American Cancer Society stated in 2019 that the link between acrylamide and cancer remains unclear, and public health bodies advise reducing heavily cooked starchy and meat foods rather than all cooked food.[10]

Fruitarianism restricts food to fruit, sometimes with nuts and seeds. Its better-known followers have included Mahatma Gandhi for about five years, and reports link Steve Jobs to fruit-based eating periods. Sources describe the diet as carrying risks of low protein, calcium, iron, zinc, B12 and vitamin D intake, and note that fruit has quickly digested sugars that raise dental and blood-sugar questions.[14]

Raw food also exists in animal-based forms, such as the raw 'primal' diet and raw meat diets, and online discussions of raw vegan eating frequently compare it with these or with animal-based diets that add lots of fruit.[9][10] Gerson therapy, a raw-juice regimen promoted as a cancer treatment, has been described as dangerous by the American Cancer Society and Cancer Research UK.[10]

In a study of long-term followers of the Hallelujah diet, a mostly raw vegan pattern, researchers measured B12 markers and followed participants given different supplement forms.[1] A cross-sectional study of sedentary people on a low-calorie, low-protein raw vegan diet reported lower cardiometabolic risk factors than comparison groups.[2]

A pilot study of guests at a raw vegan institute reported changes in quality of life and immune markers over a one- to three-week stay.[3] Research on adherence suggests the diet is hard to maintain.[6] A study of dental parameters examined periodontal and dental effects.[5] A case report described an ultra-triathlete eating raw vegan, and a paediatric case report described small bowel obstruction in a child on a strict raw vegan diet.[4][7]

In the B12 study, 49 followers of the Hallelujah diet (mostly raw fruit and vegetables, carrot juice and dehydrated barley grass juice) were tested. Six had serum B12 below 200 pg/ml, 37 (76 percent) were below 300 pg/ml, and 23 (47 percent) had abnormal urinary methylmalonic acid; sublingual B12 tablets and nutritional yeast lowered MMA while probiotic supplements did not.[1]

In the pilot study at Hippocrates Health Institute in Florida, 51 participants who completed follow-up reported overall quality of life up 11.5 percent, anxiety down 18.6 percent and perceived stress down 16.4 percent 12 weeks after a one-to-three-week stay.[3] A companion adherence study of 84 guests found that the share reporting a diet 80 percent raw rose from 16 to 28 percent over 12 weeks, and that education, disease severity and self-efficacy predicted adherence.[6]

In the dental study, 59 raw vegans and 59 controls were compared: raw vegans had better oral hygiene, similar decayed-missing-filled indices, and lower probing depth and bleeding on probing.[5] The ultra-triathlete case report found no signs of dietary deficiency in a three-time Ironman finisher on a raw vegan diet and a higher oxygen uptake at the respiratory compensation point than 10 mixed-diet Ironman athletes, with the authors calling it an open question whether a vegan diet helps or hinders endurance athletes.[4]

Wikipedia reports that a totally raw vegan diet may not supply enough vitamin B12, vitamin D or calories for a growing child and that a 2004 review linked raw diets to impaired growth and development in children.[10] It also notes that cooking can raise the availability of fat-soluble nutrients such as vitamin E and beta-carotene, and that the American Cancer Society said in 2019 the link between acrylamide and cancer was unclear.[10] A pediatric case report described acute small bowel obstruction in a child on a strict raw vegan diet.[7]

Human research is limited to small observational studies, pilot studies and case reports on nutrition, cardiometabolic markers, adherence, dental health and athletic performance.[1][2][3][4][5][6][7][16] No studies were found on skin, face or looks outcomes.

A cross-sectional study of 16 non-smoking strict raw food eaters, compared with vegans and omnivores from a German vegan-diet study, found lower BMI, body fat, energy and protein intake, lower HDL cholesterol, triglycerides, zinc and vitamin D3, and median B12 of 399 ng/L in those who supplemented against 152 ng/L in those who did not. Half the participants had homocysteine above 12 micromol/L.[16] Dietitian-authored sources note that vegan diets in general are linked with lower bone mineral density in some studies, with the clinical meaning unclear and results depending on diet quality, calcium and vitamin D intake.[15]

The British Dietetic Association has described raw veganism as a fad diet and named it on its 2018 list of celebrity diets to avoid, citing possible shortfalls of key nutrients such as B12.[10] Vegan diets in general are covered by national dietetic bodies: the Academy of Nutrition and Dietetics states that well-planned vegan diets suit all life stages, while some European bodies advise against vegan diets for infants and children without professional guidance. All the sources describe B12 from supplements or fortified foods as necessary for vegans.[15]

A 2005 study cited by Wikipedia reported low bone mass among people on long-term raw vegetarian diets, and a 2004 review linked raw diets to impaired growth in children.[10] A case report describes acute small bowel obstruction in a child on a strict raw vegan diet.[7] Eating raw plant foods carries ordinary food-safety considerations for raw sprouts and produce, and some raw foods contain compounds that cooking reduces.[10]

Media coverage in 2023 reported the death of raw vegan influencer Zhanna Samsonova, known online as Zhanna D'Art, which a New York Post report attributed to starvation according to friends; the story was discussed in bodybuilding forum threads.[17] Coverage of such cases is anecdotal, and researchers note that dietary adherence is hard to sustain for most people.[6]

On forums, raw veganism appears as one diet among many for skin and body composition. Threads on looksmax.org ask whether adopting it would improve health, and replies commonly suggest animal-based diets with lots of fruit instead, or warn that a sugar-heavy diet gives unstable energy.[9] On the bodybuilding forum T Nation, members describe mixed experiences: a user whose mother practises raw veganism and was moving to fruitarianism said he was a raw foodist for about four months, felt good at first and was lean and muscular, but called the overall experience not positive.[18]

Raw vegan influencers on social platforms promote the diet, and the 2023 news coverage of one of them was shared and debated in bodybuilding forums.[17] Influencer accounts of skin and body change are personal reports and have not been tested in trials.

lore.intro: Raw veganism is discussed on looksmaxxing and bodybuilding forums as a skin and leanness diet, usually in comparison with animal-based or fruit-heavy alternatives.[9][18]

claims.claim: Raw vegan eating improves skin and overall health.
claims.believers: Followers say uncooked plants retain enzymes and nutrients and produce clearer skin and energy.[8][9]
claims.experts: No trial tests skin outcomes. Dietetic sources say enzyme claims are not supported and note possible B12 and vitamin D shortfalls.[10][1]

claims.claim: Cooking destroys enzymes and nutrients that raw food preserves.
claims.believers: Proponents in the living-foods tradition say heating above about 40-48 degrees inactivates enzymes and reduces food value.[10][11]
claims.experts: Dietetic sources say food enzymes are digested rather than doing digestive work, and cooking raises the availability of some nutrients such as beta-carotene.[10]

claims.believers: Followers describe weight loss and a slimmer physique from a diet of low-energy-density fruit and vegetables.[18]
claims.experts: A cross-sectional study found lower BMI and body fat in strict raw food eaters, along with lower energy, protein, calcium and iodine intake.[16]

claims.claim: Raw vegans do not need B12 supplements.
claims.believers: A hypothesis tested in a study of Hallelujah-diet followers was that mostly raw fruit, vegetables and barley grass juice could avoid B12 deficiency naturally.[1]
claims.experts: In that study 76 percent of subjects had serum B12 below 300 pg/ml and 47 percent abnormal MMA; supplements lowered MMA. A later study found median B12 of 399 vs 152 ng/L in supplementing vs non-supplementing raw eaters.[1][16]

claims.claim: Raw diets are risky for children.
claims.believers: Some forum users argue instead for animal-based diets with fruit.[9]
claims.experts: A case report describes bowel obstruction in a child on a strict raw vegan diet, and a 2004 review flagged developmental concerns.[7][10]

claims.claim: An animal-based diet with fruit is preferable to raw veganism.
claims.believers: A looksmax.org reply suggests eating animal-based with lots of fruit and some vegetables instead of going vegan.[9]
claims.experts: No trial compares these diets for appearance outcomes. Wikipedia notes raw animal-food diets carry bacterial risks that cooking would remove.[10]

claims.claim: A fruit-only diet is a cleaner version of raw veganism.
claims.believers: Fruitarians say eating only fruit that falls naturally is gentler and more natural.[14]
claims.experts: Dietetic sources describe fruitarian diets as often low in protein, calcium, iron, zinc and B12, and say they are unsuitable for children and pregnant or breastfeeding women.[14]

card.summary: Uncooked plant-only eating: small studies on nutrition, none on looks, and B12 is a recurring concern.
card.note: B12 and vitamin D shortfalls reported; child cases documented.

quick.overview:
A raw vegan diet is made of uncooked plant foods kept below roughly 40-49 degrees Celsius. People in appearance communities explore it for skin and leanness.

Research is limited to small observational studies and case reports; none examined appearance.
quick.mechanism: Proponents say heat destroys enzymes and nutrients. Dietetic sources say food enzymes are digested rather than doing digestive work and that cooking can improve availability of some nutrients.
quick.risks: Reported concerns include low B12, vitamin D and calories, and case reports of problems in children.

chain: Eat uncooked plant foods and drop processed food
Higher fruit, vegetable and fibre intake at lower energy density
Followers expect clearer skin, leanness and more energy
angle.text: People follow a raw vegan diet hoping for clearer skin, leaner body composition and more energy. The diet's high fruit and vegetable content and low energy density are the practical route; studies have looked at nutrition, cardiometabolic markers and oral health rather than skin.
